dims.label: What is the main learning purpose?
dims.sub: Choose one, or two if the sequence genuinely has a dual purpose.
dims.help: Purpose drives the choice more than anything else. A misconception-focused sequence needs cognitive conflict; an argument-focused one needs structured critique; a design-focused one needs a problem with real constraints.
options: Explain a phenomenon with a model
Solve a real problem or design

dims.label: How much time do you have?
dims.help: Models that hand students control (problem-based, project-based, Ambitious Science Teaching) need time for false starts and revision. Short timeframes favour tighter sequences.
options: A depth study or term project

dims.label: How independent are your learners with inquiry?
dims.help: Novices lack the knowledge to manage open-ended tasks, so low-guidance models overload them (Kirschner, Sweller & Clark, 2006). Readiness is about experience with inquiry, not ability.

dims.label: What kind of concept is it?
dims.help: Observable phenomena suit hands-on exploration. Abstract, unobservable mechanisms (particles, genes, fields) need explicit modelling. Large-scale or historical ideas rely on data and models. Value-laden topics need ethical reasoning.

dims.label: How well known are students’ alternative conceptions?
dims.help: Robust, well-documented ideas (for example, a moving object needs a force to keep moving) call for models built around eliciting and challenging them.

dims.label: Which Working scientifically outcomes are you targeting?
dims.sub: Select all that apply (Stage 4 SC4-WS or Stage 5 SC5-WS).
dims.help: Different models build different skills. Inquiry models build planning and conducting; argument models build analysing and communicating; problem and design models build problem-solving.

dims.label: How confident are you facilitating open-ended discussion and inquiry?
dims.help: Some models ask the teacher to withhold answers, manage disagreement and follow students’ ideas. That is a learnable skill; choose a model that stretches you without derailing the class.

dims.label: What practical resources do you have?
dims.help: Some models depend on hands-on work. Without a lab, simulations (such as PhET) and secondary data sets can carry the Explore phase.

dims.label: What evidence of learning do you need?
dims.help: Align the model with the assessment. A design product suits a design cycle; a written argument suits ADI or SWH; a conceptual explanation suits 5E, GLM or Ambitious Science Teaching.

dims.label: How high are the language demands for your class?
dims.help: Classes with many EAL/D learners benefit from shared concrete experience before technical language, and from structured writing scaffolds. Talk-heavy models need extra support.

dims.label: Is there scope for place-based learning with local community?
dims.help: Some models make authentic space for local contexts and Aboriginal knowledges. Develop these with local Aboriginal community and your school’s Aboriginal Education staff.

macro.label: Unit architecture
macro.tip: Structures a whole sequence of 4–15 lessons

meso.label: Multi-lesson routine
meso.tip: An investigation or routine across a few lessons, nestable in a unit

micro.label: Single lesson
micro.tip: A strategy for one lesson or activity

dial.label: Guidance dial
dial.tip: Calibrates teacher guidance within any model

left: 5E, with structured to guided inquiry in Explore
right: Interactive Approach, or open inquiry in a depth study

purposePhrase.model: build an explanatory model of a phenomenon
purposePhrase.design: solve a real problem or design a solution

models.name: 5E
models.distinct: A balanced default with an explicit Explain phase after inquiry.
models.fit: Most Stage 4–5 focus areas; the strongest default for early career teachers.
models.teacher: Facilitates Engage and Explore, teaches explicitly in Explain, designs transfer in Elaborate, and assesses throughout.
models.learner: Predicts, investigates, explains with evidence, applies ideas in new contexts, and reflects on how their thinking changed.
models.pitfall: Relabelling existing lessons with E headings without changing their order.
models.evidence: A 2023 meta-analysis of 61 randomised trials found large gains in science achievement for 3E/5E/7E models (g = 0.87).

models.name: Argument-Driven Inquiry
models.distinct: Argument and peer critique are built into the investigation itself.
models.fit: Stage 5 investigations targeting SC5-WS-08; Reactions, Waves and motion, Environmental sustainability.
models.teacher: Frames the guiding question and the criteria, approves plans for safety rather than correctness, models critique language, consolidates the science, and holds reviewers accountable.
models.learner: Designs the investigation, builds a three-part argument, critiques and is critiqued, writes an individual report, reviews a peer's report, and revises their own.
models.pitfall: Dropping the argumentation session or peer review when time runs short, which removes the core.
models.evidence: Quasi-experimental studies report gains in argument writing and science proficiency, with the strongest effects when critique is genuinely two-way.
phases: Design the method and collect data

models.name: Levels of inquiry
models.distinct: Not a sequence but a way to calibrate how much of the investigation the teacher specifies.
models.fit: Any practical work; planning a progression of independence from Stage 4 to Stage 5.
models.teacher: Decides which of the question, the method and the result to specify, then fades that support deliberately across a unit and a stage.
models.learner: Takes on more of the framing, design and interpretation as routines and content knowledge build.
models.pitfall: Jumping to open inquiry with novices, or never moving beyond confirmation.
models.evidence: A planning framework rather than a tested model, but the direction it points is well supported: guided inquiry outperforms both unguided discovery and verification practicals, and teacher-led activities outperformed student-led ones by about 0.40 in Furtak et al.'s meta-analysis.

models.name: Predict–Observe–Explain
models.distinct: Creates and uses cognitive conflict within a single lesson.
models.fit: Discrepant events with a clear, visible outcome: dissolving and mass, falling objects, living and non-living, hygiene and microbes.
models.teacher: Chooses a genuinely discrepant event, protects the prediction from cueing, makes the observation clear and checkable, and orchestrates reconciliation before consolidating the science.
models.learner: Commits to a prediction with reasons, observes carefully, compares prediction with observation, and revises their explanation.
models.pitfall: Running the demonstration before predictions are committed in writing, or skipping the explain step.
models.evidence: Widely used as a diagnostic and conceptual-change strategy; evidence is mainly classroom-based. Anomalous data does not change ideas on its own, so the explain step carries the learning.

models.name: Learning cycle
models.distinct: The minimal experience-before-vocabulary sequence, and the ancestor of 5E.
models.fit: Short concept sequences built on a clear lab phenomenon.
models.teacher: Designs the exploration, then introduces terms at the moment students need them.
models.learner: Explores, attaches new terms to experience, then applies them.
models.pitfall: Introducing terms before exploration, which collapses it into a traditional lesson.
models.evidence: Early studies (for example, Abraham & Renner, 1986) supported the sequence; it is included in 3E/5E/7E meta-analyses.

models.name: 7E
models.distinct: Separates eliciting prior knowledge from engaging interest, and adds far transfer.
models.fit: Topics with robust misconceptions and clear real-world transfer, such as Energy and Disease.
models.teacher: Diagnoses prior knowledge deliberately and designs a far-transfer task.
models.learner: Surfaces their own ideas and extends learning to unfamiliar contexts.
models.pitfall: Treating Elicit as a quick brainstorm whose results are never used.
models.evidence: Pooled with 5E in meta-analyses; the added phases rest on strong prior-knowledge and transfer research.

models.name: Generative Learning Model
phases: Challenge: compare with peers’ and scientists’ views
models.distinct: Makes the challenge between student and scientific views the centrepiece.
models.fit: Stubborn intuitive ideas: forces and motion, plant nutrition, heat and temperature.
models.teacher: Investigates students’ ideas first, then stages a respectful challenge.
models.learner: Clarifies, defends and revises their view against evidence.
models.pitfall: A ‘challenge’ that is really a correction, so students defer rather than reason.
models.evidence: Developed through the New Zealand Learning in Science Project; evidence is mainly classroom-based and qualitative.

models.name: CASE (Thinking Science)
models.distinct: Targets general reasoning patterns (control of variables, proportionality, probability, classification) rather than topic content.
models.fit: Stage 4 reasoning foundations that underpin planning (WS-03) and analysis (WS-06).
models.teacher: Manages conflict and group talk, withholds answers, and prompts reflection and bridging.
models.learner: Reasons aloud, reflects on how they thought, and transfers the pattern.
models.pitfall: Rushing to the right answer, which removes the conflict the lesson depends on.
models.evidence: Early UK studies reported lasting gains; a later large UK trial of the Let’s Think programme found no attainment effect, so implementation quality matters.

models.name: Interactive Approach
models.distinct: Students’ own questions drive the investigations.
models.fit: Local environments, Living systems and depth studies.
models.teacher: Elicits and sorts students’ questions, helping them become investigable.
models.learner: Generates questions and designs investigations to answer them.
models.pitfall: Collecting students’ questions and then answering them by lecture.
models.evidence: Originated in primary science; evidence is mainly classroom-based and qualitative.

models.name: Science Writing Heuristic
models.distinct: A writing-to-learn scaffold that turns lab reports into reasoning.
models.fit: Any practical; particularly strong in EAL/D-rich classes. Builds WS-06 and WS-08.
models.teacher: Negotiates meaning in discussion and prompts comparison with the literature.
models.learner: Writes questions, claims and evidence, and reflects on how their thinking changed.
models.pitfall: Using the template as a fill-in form without the class negotiation of claims.
models.evidence: Multiple studies report gains, often largest for lower-achieving students.

models.name: Ambitious Science Teaching
models.distinct: Students’ explanatory models are drafted early and revised publicly across the unit.
models.fit: Unobservable mechanisms: particles, cells, genetics, climate, disease transmission.
models.teacher: Selects the anchoring phenomenon, then tracks and presses on students’ models.
models.learner: Drafts, tests and revises explanatory models in public.
models.pitfall: An anchoring phenomenon too thin to sustain a unit, or models that are never revised.
models.evidence: A growing body of classroom and design-based research; fewer controlled trials.

models.name: Problem-based learning
phases: What we know and need to know
models.distinct: The problem comes first; content is learned in order to solve it.
models.fit: Environmental sustainability, Disease, Materials; best with experienced learners.
models.teacher: Tutor and cognitive coach who manages the process rather than delivering content.
models.pitfall: Too little scaffolding, so novices flounder and misconceptions persist.
models.evidence: Mixed in school science; effective when strongly scaffolded (Hmelo-Silver, Duncan & Chinn, 2007).

models.name: Project-based science
models.distinct: Extended, artefact-producing work around a driving question.
models.teacher: Designs the driving question and scaffolds sustained inquiry.
models.learner: Investigator and producer of public artefacts.
models.pitfall: A product that can be completed without the science.
models.evidence: Promising results from well-designed curricula; outcomes vary with design and support.

models.name: Engineering design cycle
models.src: Various (for example, ask, imagine, plan, create, test, improve)
models.distinct: Success is a working solution, not an explanation.
models.teacher: Sets constraints and criteria, and coaches iteration.
models.learner: Designer who tests, fails and improves.
models.pitfall: Trial and error with no science used to justify design choices.
models.evidence: Integrated STEM evidence is varied; stronger when science concepts are explicitly required.

models.name: SSI-based teaching
models.distinct: Integrates values and ethics with scientific evidence.
models.fit: Genetics, Energy, Environmental sustainability, Data science 2.
models.teacher: Frames a contested issue, keeps the science sound, and facilitates respectful deliberation.
models.learner: Evaluates evidence and weighs values to reach a justified position.
models.pitfall: A debate built on opinion with thin science underneath.
models.evidence: Research shows gains in argumentation and reasoning; content gains vary.
